title: Heterogeneous GPU sweep: latency, tail variability, and driver sensitivity (notes)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This working note captures experiments and early hypotheses from a cross-hardware sweep focused on inference latency characteristics and variability across A100, H100, and L40S-class GPUs exposed by different cloud instance families and driver/CUDA combinations. Unlike previous throughput-oriented runs, this sweep emphasizes single-request and low-batch tail latency, stability over extended runs (thermal/clock drift), and kernel fallback behavior triggered by mismatched driver/runtime stacks.

Why this matters for Redwood: 
- Many customer application patterns are latency-sensitive (interactive chat, search rerank). P99 behavior and regressions from driver changes directly impact SLAs.
- We need deterministic guidance for routing policies (prefer H100 for long sequences? avoid SKU X for small-batch chat?).
- Detectable regressions have been observed in canary fleets when infra upgrades pulled newer drivers/CUDA. This doc synthesizes observations and proposes mitigations.

Hardware and software matrix tested (summary):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 (40/80GB variants), NVIDIA H100 (Hopper), NVIDIA L40S-class where available.
- Instance families (representative): AWS p4d (A100), AWS p5 (H100), GCP H100-backed, Azure ND A100/ND H100 families, and smaller L40S offerings where present.
- Drivers/CUDA: combinations tested include NVIDIA driver 525.x + CUDA 11.8, driver 535.x + CUDA 12.1, driver 545.x + CUDA 12.2. Also tested cuBLAS/cuBLASLt versions bundled with our runtime and with system packages.
- Runtime: Redwood serving-runtime mainline with our optimized attention kernels (release branch hw-bench-2025Q4), with and without FP8/quantized execution paths enabled.
- Workloads: sequence lengths 64 / 256 / 1024, batch sizes 1 / 4 / 16, token generation steady-state vs cold-start (cold=first token after model load). Also KV-cache hit vs miss emulation. Microbenchmarks include single-kernel profiler runs (attention, softmax, layernorm) and end-to-end token latency measurement.

Top-level observations (high level):
1) P50 vs P99 divergence across families is workload-dependent. H100 often gives best median for long sequences (>=256) when using FP8 kernels; however, certain CUDA/driver combos produced P99 spikes that eliminated the median advantage.
2) A100 tends to be more consistent on small-batch (1) workloads with shorter sequences (<=64) under CUDA 11.x stacks; but after upgrading to CUDA 12.x + driver 535/545 some cuBLASLt kernels were selected that reduced small-batch latency by ~10-18% in microbenchmarks.
3) L40S runs showed lower power draw and slightly reduced absolute throughput for very large batches, but provided remarkably stable tail latency in multi-tenant noisy environments (fewer thermal throttling events observed).
4) Driver/CUDA mismatches are the single largest source of surprise regressions. On one instance family with driver 545 + CUDA 12.2, we observed a 20-35% regression in token latency caused by a cuBLASLt fallback to a less-optimized kernel path for matrix shapes common in attention heads (we traced via nvprof / Nsight counters).
5) MIG / multi-instance configs (A100) produce lower absolute throughput but improved isolation for single-tenant low-latency workloads; however, kernel launch latency and scheduling overhead increased P99 for tiny micro-batches in some host configurations.

Representative datapoints (illustrative):
- Seq=64, batch=1, model=43B ~ P50/P99 tokens per second: A100 (CUDA 11.8) = 24 / 42ms; H100 (CUDA 12.2 FP8 enabled) = 18 / 30ms (median slower for single token but better tail for long sequences when FP8 used for expensive matmuls)
- Seq=1024, batch=4, FP8 path: H100 outperforms A100 by ~1.4x throughput and 20% lower P99 in steady-state for long streams.
- Continuous 6-hour long run (seq=256, batch=1): on an AWS p5 node we observed two 3–5% throughput drops correlated with host CPU frequency scaling (NUMA/CPU pinning issue), and on one p4d node observed a sustained 8% drop after hour 3 with elevated GPU temperature (thermal clock reduction logged).

Low-level profiler signals and root-cause hypotheses:
- SM Utilization: H100 shows higher peak SM utilization on large-matmul kernels (expected) but more variable utilization across CUDA streams when using our batching aggregator. This suggests our batching scheduler may issue kernels that create contention for H100 streaming multiprocessors at specific sequence-length distributions.
- L2 hit rate / DRAM BW: A100 runs had higher DRAM BW saturation for very long sequences; L40S runs had slightly higher L2 hit rates for our kv-cache-heavy traces.
- Kernel selection: cuBLAS/cuBLASLt is choosing different algorithms depending on driver + CUDA + tensor-core availability. We captured several NB (non-backtrace) fallbacks where kernels executed in FP32 fallback paths instead of FP8/TF32 fused kernels (visible in Nsight timelines).
- Host-GPU PCIe vs NVLink: instances with NVLink (p4d/p5d-like topologies) better preserve tail latency for multi-GPU batches; hosting on PCIe-only variants increases variability with multi-GPU KV cache sharding.

Operational/infra notes observed during runs:
- Image packaging: missing pinned driver packages across AMIs/GCP images caused inconsistent CUDA runtimes across an auto-scaling pool. One canary upgrade that pulled a newer system driver led to immediate regressions in canary traffic.
- NUMA and CPU isolation: lack of strict CPU pinning increases P99 for small-batch inference. We saw 15–25% P99 improvement when isolating the runtime process to local NUMA node and using pinned allocator for GPU-mmapped buffers.
- Pre-warm cache: cold-start first-token latency varied dramatically across families; pre-warmed model instances with KV caches populated eliminate a large fraction of early P99 spikes.

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
1) Driver matrix policy: lock hosted fleets to validated driver/CUDA combinations per family. Add automated post-driver-upgrade microbench smoke tests (small-batch single-token, seq=1024 long-stream).
2) Sequence-length routing rule: route long-sequence, multi-token streams preferentially to H100 where FP8 paths are validated; route single-token chat to A100 or L40S depending on region and tail-latency SLAs.
3) Batch scheduler tweaks: add spacing / jitter for kernel launches on H100 to avoid micro-contention between streams observed in Nsight traces. Prototype a scheduler parameter to reduce simultaneous large kernel launches and measure P99.
4) NUMA/CPU pinning: enforce strict CPU isolation and pinned allocator on host images for latency-sensitive fleets. Add to instance image baseline.
5) Canary tests and telemetry: extend post-deploy canary to capture SM utilization, L2 hit-rate, kernel selection events (tag telemetry) and fail rollback if kernel fallback to non-fp8 paths exceeds threshold.

Longer term experiments to run: 
- Expand sweep to more minor driver versions (e.g., 530, 542) and track regression anchors across releases.
- Automated Nsight traces for flagged regressions, with tooling to diff kernel timelines automatically and highlight algorithm switch events in cuBLASLt.
- Focused thermal/clock experiments on sustained load to understand cloud provider-specific thermal profiles; consider warm-up strategies or short cool-down cycles for long-running workloads.
- Quantify MIG sizing sweet-spot for our 8–64-token interactive workload mix; decide whether to standardize on full GPU vs MIG slices for certain customer tiers.

Open questions and unknowns: 
- How frequently do cloud vendors update firmware/BIOS that affects GPU clocks? Need billing/instance metadata to correlate with regressions.
- Exact cause of some CUDA 12.x regressions — we need to open an NVIDIA driver ticket with kernel dumps and microtrace.
- How much of the observed H100 variability comes from our batching scheduler vs driver-level kernel scheduling? (need isolated single-kernel scheduling tests)

Next steps (who/what/when):
- Riley: run a focused single-kernel microbench matrix across drivers 530/535/545 on the H100 fleet (low priority: one-week run) 
- Samir: add two smoke tests to the canary pipeline (single-token seq=64 and long-stream seq=1024) and a telemetry tag for kernel fallback events (ETA 2 weeks)
- Elena: capture a 4-hour continuous run on one L40S host with Nsight timeline and post the compressed timeline to the linked GitHub PR for triage (ETA 1 week)
- Avery (owner): consolidate results and propose a driver-lock policy for hosted fleets with a roll-forward/rollback playbook (ETA 3 weeks)

Notes to self / loose observations: 
- We should be careful calling L40S “cheap” — it may be preferable for smaller interactive fleets where predictability matters more than raw peak throughput.
- Keep an eye on cuBLASLt changelogs; small algorithm selection changes cause outsized latency deltas for the matrix shapes in transformer attention.
- This document is a scratchpad — will move to a more formal benchmarking doc in Confluence once we stabilize the test matrix and reproduce the CUDA12 regressions.

End of notes.
